{{Short description|Fairness notion in fair item allocation}}
'''Envy-freeness up to any''' '''item (EFX)''' is a fairness notion in [[fair item allocation]]. It is a relaxation of [[envy-free item allocation]]. Determining whether EFX allocations always exist is widely regarded as the central open problem in the theory of fair item allocation.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal |last1=Procaccia |first1=Ariel D. |title=Technical perspective: An answer to fair division's most enigmatic question |journal=Communications of the ACM |date=20 March 2020 |volume=63 |issue=4 |pages=118 |doi=10.1145/3382131 }}</ref>

== Background ==
{{unsolved|computer science|Does there exist an envy-free up to any item allocation for four or more agents with additive valuations?}}In the classical fair division problem, a set of indivisible items must be allocated among a group of agents, each with their own preferences over subsets of items. An allocation assigns every item to exactly one agent. A valuation function describes how agent ''i'' values any bundle of items. Valuations are typically assumed to be [[Monotone set function|monotone]] (adding items never decreases value) and often [[Additive utility|additive]] (the value of a bundle equals the sum of the values of its items).

An allocation is [[Envy-free item allocation|envy-free]] (EF) if no agent prefers another agent's bundle to their own. Envy-free allocations do not always exist when items are indivisible — for instance, a single valuable item cannot be shared between two agents without creating envy. This motivates the study of relaxations of fairness notions.

A standard relaxation is '''envy-freeness up to one good''' ('''EF1'''), introduced by Budish:<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Budish |first1=Eric |title=The Combinatorial Assignment Problem: Approximate Competitive Equilibrium from Equal Incomes |journal=Journal of Political Economy |date=December 2011 |volume=119 |issue=6 |pages=1061–1103 |doi=10.1086/664613 }}</ref> an allocation is EF1 if any envy agent ''i'' has toward agent ''j'' can be eliminated by hypothetically removing ''some'' single item from ''j''<nowiki />'s bundle. EF1 allocations always exist and can be computed in polynomial time (see [[envy-free item allocation]]).

== Definition ==
'''Envy-freeness up to any good (EFX)''' is a strictly stronger notion than EF1. It was introduced in 2016 by Caragiannis, Kurokawa, [[Hervé Moulin|Moulin]], [[Ariel D. Procaccia|Proaccia]], Shah and Wang<ref>{{cite book |last1=Caragiannis |first1=Ioannis |last2=Kurokawa |first2=David |last3=Moulin |first3=Hervé |last4=Procaccia |first4=Ariel D. |last5=Shah |first5=Nisarg |last6=Wang |first6=Junxing |title=Proceedings of the 2016 ACM Conference on Economics and Computation |chapter=The Unreasonable Fairness of Maximum Nash Welfare |date=2016 |pages=305–322 |doi=10.1145/2940716.2940726 |isbn=978-1-4503-3936-0 }}</ref><ref name=":1">{{cite journal |last1=Caragiannis |first1=Ioannis |last2=Kurokawa |first2=David |last3=Moulin |first3=Hervé |last4=Procaccia |first4=Ariel D. |last5=Shah |first5=Nisarg |last6=Wang |first6=Junxing |title=The Unreasonable Fairness of Maximum Nash Welfare |journal=ACM Transactions on Economics and Computation |date=31 August 2019 |volume=7 |issue=3 |pages=1–32 |doi=10.1145/3355902 }}</ref> in their study of maximum Nash welfare allocations. An allocation is '''EFX''' if for every pair of agents ''i'' and ''j'', and for every item ''g'' in ''j''<nowiki />'s bundle that agent ''i'' values positively, removing ''g'' from ''j''<nowiki />'s bundle would eliminate ''i''<nowiki />'s envy.

In contrast to EF1, which requires only the existence of ''some'' item whose removal eliminates envy, EFX requires that removing ''any'' positively valued item from the envied bundle would suffice. The good is not actually removed — this is a thought experiment used to define the fairness condition.

Caragiannis et al. described EFX as "arguably the best fairness analog of envy-freeness for indivisible items."<ref name=":1" /> The question of whether EFX allocations always exist was immediately recognized as a fundamental open problem, and has been called "fair division's most enigmatic question."<ref name=":0" />

== Existence for two agents ==
The first general existence result for EFX was established by Plaut and [[Tim Roughgarden|Roughgarden]] in 2018.<ref name=":6">{{cite book |last1=Plaut |first1=Benjamin |last2=Roughgarde |first2=Tim |title=Proceedings of the Twenty-Ninth Annual ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms |chapter=Almost Envy-Freeness with General Valuations |date=2018 |pages=2584–2603 |doi=10.1137/1.9781611975031.165 |arxiv=1707.04769 |isbn=978-1-61197-503-1 }}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Plaut |first1=Benjamin |last2=Roughgarden |first2=Tim |date=January 2020 |title=Almost Envy-Freeness with General Valuations |journal=SIAM Journal on Discrete Mathematics |volume=34 |issue=2 |pages=1039–1068 |doi=10.1137/19m124397x |arxiv=1707.04769 }}</ref> They showed that an EFX allocation always exists for two agents with arbitrary monotone valuations, via a simple adaptation of the classical [[Divide and choose|cut-and-choose protocol]]. Agent 1 splits all items into two bundles so as to maximize her minimum value across the two bundles — that is, she finds the partition that makes the worse bundle as valuable as possible from her own perspective. Agent 2 then picks whichever bundle she prefers, and agent 1 receives the other.

The key observation is that this optimal split guarantees both bundles are EFX-feasible for agent 1: if removing any single item from either bundle left that bundle strictly more valuable than the other, agent 1 could have moved that item across beforehand and obtained a better-balanced partition — contradicting optimality. Since this holds for both bundles, agent 1 is EFX-satisfied no matter which bundle agent 2 takes. Agent 2, having chosen her favorite bundle, does not envy agent 1 at all, and is therefore EFX-satisfied trivially.

In contrast to EF1, which requires a number of queries logarithmic in the number of items, computing an EFX allocation may require a linear number of queries even when there are two agents with identical additive valuations.<ref name=":02">{{cite journal |last1=Oh |first1=Hoon |last2=Procaccia |first2=Ariel D. |last3=Suksompong |first3=Warut |title=Fairly Allocating Many Goods with Few Queries |journal=Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence |date=17 July 2019 |volume=33 |issue=1 |pages=2141–2148 |doi=10.1609/aaai.v33i01.33012141 |doi-access=free |arxiv=1807.11367 }}</ref> For two agents with general monotone valuations, computing an EFX allocation may require an exponential number of queries.<ref name=":6" /><ref name=":2" />

Another difference between EF1 and EFX is that the number of EFX allocations can be as few as 2 (for two agents and any number of items), while the number of EF1 allocations is always exponential in the number of items.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Suksompong |first1=Warut |title=On the number of almost envy-free allocations |journal=Discrete Applied Mathematics |date=September 2020 |volume=284 |pages=606–610 |doi=10.1016/j.dam.2020.03.039 |arxiv=2006.00178 }}</ref>

== Existence for three agents ==
The existence of EFX allocations for three or more agents with non-identical valuations was a major open problem, noted by Plaut and Roughgarden as "highly non-trivial even for three players with different additive valuations."<ref name=":2" />

A breakthrough<ref>{{cite book |last1=Amanatidis |first1=Georgios |last2=Birmpas |first2=Georgios |last3=Filos-Ratsikas |first3=Aris |last4=Voudouris |first4=Alexandros A. |title=Proceedings of the Thirty-First International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence |chapter=Fair Division of Indivisible Goods: A Survey |date=2022 |pages=5385–5393 |doi=10.24963/ijcai.2022/756 |isbn=978-1-956792-00-3 }}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last1=Amanatidis |first1=Georgios |last2=Aziz |first2=Haris |last3=Birmpas |first3=Georgios |last4=Filos-Ratsikas |first4=Aris |last5=Li |first5=Bo |last6=Moulin |first6=Hervé |last7=Voudouris |first7=Alexandros A. |last8=Wu |first8=Xiaowei |date=September 2023 |title=Fair division of indivisible goods: Recent progress and open questions |journal=Artificial Intelligence |volume=322 |article-number=103965 |doi=10.1016/j.artint.2023.103965 |hdl=10397/108447 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Gollapudi |first1=Sreenivas |last2=Kollias |first2=Kostas |last3=Plaut |first3=Benjamin |title=Web and Internet Economics |chapter=Almost Envy-Free Repeated Matching in Two-Sided Markets |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |date=2020 |volume=12495 |pages=3–16 |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-64946-3_1 |arxiv=2009.09336 |isbn=978-3-030-64945-6 }}</ref> was established at 2020 by Chaudhury, Garg, and [[Kurt Mehlhorn|Mehlhorn]],<ref name=":7">{{cite book |last1=Chaudhury |first1=Bhaskar Ray |last2=Garg |first2=Jugal |last3=Mehlhorn |first3=Kurt |title=Proceedings of the 21st ACM Conference on Economics and Computation |chapter=EFX Exists for Three Agents |date=2020 |pages=1–19 |doi=10.1145/3391403.3399511 |isbn=978-1-4503-7975-5 }}</ref><ref name=":8">{{cite journal |last1=Chaudhury |first1=Bhaskar Ray |last2=Garg |first2=Jugal |last3=Mehlhorn |first3=Kurt |title=EFX Exists for Three Agents |journal=Journal of the ACM |date=29 February 2024 |volume=71 |issue=1 |pages=1–27 |doi=10.1145/3616009 }}</ref> who proved that an EFX allocation always exists for three agents with additive valuations. The core difficulty compared to the two-agent case is that any transfer of goods between two agents' bundles inevitably affects the third agent's envy relationships as well — a change that fixes one agent's envy may create or worsen another's. The proof maintains a partial EFX allocation in which some goods may be left temporarily unallocated, and resolves envy by a combination of transfers along envy cycles and carefully controlled augmentations from the unallocated pool, tracked by a lexicographic potential function that strictly increases at each step and guarantees termination. The argument makes heavy use of the additive structure of the valuations and does not extend to four or more agents.

The result was subsequently extended and simplified by Akrami, [[Noga Alon|Alon]], Chaudhury, Garg, Mehlhorn, and Mehta,<ref>{{cite book |last1=Akrami |first1=Hannaneh |last2=Alon |first2=Noga |last3=Chaudhury |first3=Bhaskar Ray |last4=Garg |first4=Jugal |last5=Mehlhorn |first5=Kurt |last6=Mehta |first6=Ruta |title=Proceedings of the 24th ACM Conference on Economics and Computation |chapter=EFX: A Simpler Approach and an (Almost) Optimal Guarantee via Rainbow Cycle Number |date=2023 |page=61 |doi=10.1145/3580507.3597799 |isbn=979-8-4007-0104-7 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Akrami |first1=Hannaneh |last2=Alon |first2=Noga |last3=Chaudhury |first3=Bhaskar Ray |last4=Garg |first4=Jugal |last5=Mehlhorn |first5=Kurt |last6=Mehta |first6=Ruta |date=March 2025 |title=EFX: A Simpler Approach and an (Almost) Optimal Guarantee via Rainbow Cycle Number |journal=Operations Research |volume=73 |issue=2 |pages=738–751 |doi=10.1287/opre.2023.0433 }}</ref>  who showed it holds even when two of the three agents have arbitrary monotone valuations and only one is required to be additive.

Both algorithms run in [[pseudo-polynomial time]] (polynomial in the number of items and the highest utility an agent assigns to an item). Whether a polynomial-time algorithm exists remains an open question.<ref name=":3" />

== Approximations, relaxations, and special cases ==
Since exact EFX allocations are not known to always exist for general instances, a substantial body of work has focused on approximations, relaxations, and restricted settings.

=== Multiplicative approximation ===
For a parameter α ∈ [0,1], an allocation is '''α-EFX''' if for every pair of agents ''i'' and ''j'' and every positively valued item ''g'' in ''j''<nowiki />'s bundle, agent ''i''<nowiki />'s value for their own bundle is at least α times their value for ''j''<nowiki />'s bundle after removing ''g''. Thus 1-EFX coincides with exact EFX, and larger α corresponds to a stronger guarantee.

A 1/2-approximate EFX allocation (that also satisfies a different approximate-fairness notion called ''Maximin Aware'') can be found in polynomial time.<ref>{{cite arXiv|last1=Chan|first1=Hau|last2=Chen|first2=Jing|last3=Li|first3=Bo|last4=Wu|first4=Xiaowei|date=2019-10-25|title=Maximin-Aware Allocations of Indivisible Goods|class=cs.GT|eprint=1905.09969}}</ref>

The best known approximation for general additive valuations is (φ − 1) ≈ 0.618-EFX, where φ = (1+√5)/2 is the golden ratio, achieved via a variant of the [[envy-graph procedure]] in polynomial time. Their algorithm also guarantees EF1 and an 2/(φ+2) approximation to group [[maximin share]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Amanatidis |first1=Georgios |last2=Markakis |first2=Evangelos |last3=Ntokos |first3=Apostolos |title=Multiple Birds with One Stone: Beating 1/2 for EFX and GMMS via Envy Cycle Elimination |journal=Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence |date=3 April 2020 |volume=34 |issue=2 |pages=1790–1797 |doi=10.1609/aaai.v34i02.5545 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Amanatidis |first1=Georgios |last2=Markakis |first2=Evangelos |last3=Ntokos |first3=Apostolos |date=12 November 2020 |title=Multiple birds with one stone: Beating 1/2 for EFX and GMMS via envy cycle elimination |journal=Theoretical Computer Science |volume=841 |pages=94–109 |doi=10.1016/j.tcs.2020.07.006 |arxiv=1909.07650 }}</ref>

Improving beyond the (φ − 1) factor remains an important open problem. Under additional ordinal assumptions — specifically, when agents agree on which ''n'' items are the most valuable — a 2/3-EFX allocation was shown to exist.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Markakis |first1=Evangelos |last2=Santorinaios |first2=Christodoulos |title=Proceedings of the Third International Joint Conference on Autonomous Agents and Multiagent Systems - Volume 1 |chapter=Improved EFX Approximation Guarantees under Ordinal-based Assumptions |date=2023 |pages=591–599 |doi=10.65109/njfc3604 |isbn=978-1-58113-864-1 }}</ref>

=== EFX with charity ===
A natural relaxation allows some goods to remain unallocated, donated to a "charity". Obviously, donating all items yields an envy-free allocation, which is trivially EFX. The challenge is to attain EFX together with some welfare guarantees.

Caragiannis, Gravin and Huang proved that, when all agents have additive valuations, there exists a partial EFX allocation that achieves at least half of the maximum [[Nash welfare]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Caragiannis |first1=Ioannis |last2=Gravin |first2=Nick |last3=Huang |first3=Xin |title=Proceedings of the 2019 ACM Conference on Economics and Computation |chapter=Envy-Freeness up to Any Item with High Nash Welfare: The Virtue of Donating Items |date=2019 |pages=527–545 |doi=10.1145/3328526.3329574 |isbn=978-1-4503-6792-9 }}</ref>

This was strengthened to show that a partial EFX allocation with at most ''n''−1 unallocated goods always exists for any number of agents with general monotone valuations (for additive valuations, this allocation also attains at least half of the maximum Nash welfare).<ref>{{cite book |last1=Chaudhury |first1=Bhaskar Ray |last2=Kavitha |first2=Telikepalli |last3=Mehlhorn |first3=Kurt |last4=Sgouritsa |first4=Alkmini |title=Proceedings of the Fourteenth Annual ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms |chapter=A Little Charity Guarantees Almost Envy-Freeness |date=2020 |pages=2658–2672 |doi=10.1137/1.9781611975994.162 |arxiv=1907.04596 |isbn=978-1-61197-599-4 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chaudhury |first1=Bhaskar Ray |last2=Kavitha |first2=Telikepalli |last3=Mehlhorn |first3=Kurt |last4=Sgouritsa |first4=Alkmini |date=January 2021 |title=A Little Charity Guarantees Almost Envy-Freeness |journal=SIAM Journal on Computing |volume=50 |issue=4 |pages=1336–1358 |doi=10.1137/20m1359134 |arxiv=1907.04596 }}</ref>

Subsequently, it was shown that four agents always admit an EFX allocation with at most one unallocated good, and ''n'' ≥ 5 agents with at most ''n''−2 unallocated goods.<ref name=":9">{{cite journal |last1=Berger |first1=Ben |last2=Cohen |first2=Avi |last3=Feldman |first3=Michal |last4=Fiat |first4=Amos |title=Almost Full EFX Exists for Four Agents |journal=Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence |date=28 June 2022 |volume=36 |issue=5 |pages=4826–4833 |doi=10.1609/aaai.v36i5.20410 }}</ref>

=== Rainbow cycle number ===
An elegant connection between approximate EFX allocations and a combinatorial graph-theoretic problem called the [[rainbow cycle number]] was introduced.<ref name=":4">{{cite book |last1=Chaudhury |first1=Bhaskar Ray |last2=Garg |first2=Jugal |last3=Mehlhorn |first3=Kurt |last4=Mehta |first4=Ruta |last5=Misra |first5=Pranabendu |title=Proceedings of the 22nd ACM Conference on Economics and Computation |chapter=Improving EFX Guarantees through Rainbow Cycle Number |date=2021 |pages=310–311 |doi=10.1145/3465456.3467605 |isbn=978-1-4503-8554-1 }}</ref><ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last1=Chaudhury |first1=Bhaskar Ray |last2=Garg |first2=Jugal |last3=Mehlhorn |first3=Kurt |last4=Mehta |first4=Ruta |last5=Misra |first5=Pranabendu |date=November 2024 |title=Improving Envy Freeness up to Any Good Guarantees Through Rainbow Cycle Number |journal=Mathematics of Operations Research |volume=49 |issue=4 |pages=2323–2340 |doi=10.1287/moor.2021.0252 }}</ref> For a given integer ''d'', the rainbow cycle number ''R''(''d'') is the largest ''k'' such that there exists a ''k''-partite directed graph satisfying: (1) every part has at most ''d'' vertices; (2) for every pair of parts ''i'' and ''j'', each vertex in ''i'' has an incoming edge from some vertex in ''j''; and (3) the graph contains no rainbow cycle — that is, no directed cycle that visits each part at most once. It was shown that bounding the rainbow cycle number polynomially in ''d'' yields approximate EFX allocations with sublinearly many unallocated goods. The initial bound gave (1−ε)-EFX existence with ''O''((''n''/ε)<sup>4/5</sup>) unallocated goods, for any ε>0.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":5" /> A subsequent near-linear bound on the rainbow cycle number tightened this to Õ((''n''/ε)<sup>1/2</sup>) unallocated goods.<ref name=":10">{{Cite journal |last1=Akrami |first1=Hannaneh |last2=Alon |first2=Noga |last3=Chaudhury |first3=Bhaskar Ray |last4=Garg |first4=Jugal |last5=Mehlhorn |first5=Kurt |last6=Mehta |first6=Ruta |date=March–April 2025 |title=EFX: A Simpler Approach and an (Almost) Optimal Guarantee via Rainbow Cycle Number |journal=Operations Research |volume=73 |issue=2 |pages=738–751 |doi=10.1287/opre.2023.0433 }}</ref><ref name=":11">{{cite book |last1=Akrami |first1=Hannaneh |last2=Alon |first2=Noga |last3=Chaudhury |first3=Bhaskar Ray |last4=Garg |first4=Jugal |last5=Mehlhorn |first5=Kurt |last6=Mehta |first6=Ruta |title=Proceedings of the 24th ACM Conference on Economics and Computation |chapter=EFX: A Simpler Approach and an (Almost) Optimal Guarantee via Rainbow Cycle Number |date=2023 |page=61 |doi=10.1145/3580507.3597799 |isbn=979-8-4007-0104-7 }}</ref>

It remains open whether an EFX allocation exists with a sub-linear number of unallocated goods.<ref name=":3" />

=== Removing more items ===
For any positive integer ''k'', EF''k''X is a weakening of EFX allowing removal of up to any ''k'' items.

EF2X allocations are known to exist for ''n''=4 agents with additive valuations.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ashuri |first1=Arash |last2=Gkatzelis |first2=Vasilis |last3=Sgouritsa |first3=Alkmini |title=EF2X Exists for Four Agents |journal=Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence |date=11 April 2025 |volume=39 |issue=13 |pages=13555–13563 |doi=10.1609/aaai.v39i13.33480 |doi-access=free }}</ref> For ''restricted additive'' valuations — where each agent values every good at either 0 or a good-specific amount — EF2X allocations were shown to always exist.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Akrami |first1=Hannaneh |last2=Rezvan |first2=Rojin |last3=Seddighin |first3=Masoud |title=Proceedings of the Thirty-First International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence |chapter=An EF2X Allocation Protocol for Restricted Additive Valuations |date=2022 |pages=17–23 |doi=10.24963/ijcai.2022/3 |isbn=978-1-956792-00-3 }}</ref>

It remains open whether there is any constant ''k'' such that EF''k''X allocations exist for all ''n'' and all additive valuations.

=== Special cases ===
EFX allocations are also known to exist in several restricted valuation settings. When each agent's value for every item takes one of at most two possible values, the maximum Nash welfare allocation is always EFX, and an explicit polynomial-time algorithm was given.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Amanatidis |first1=Georgios |last2=Birmpas |first2=Georgios |last3=Filos-Ratsikas |first3=Aris |last4=Hollender |first4=Alexandros |last5=Voudouris |first5=Alexandros A. |title=Proceedings of the Twenty-Ninth International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence |chapter=Maximum Nash Welfare and Other Stories About EFX |date=2020 |pages=24–30 |doi=10.24963/ijcai.2020/4 |isbn=978-0-9992411-6-5 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Amanatidis |first1=Georgios |last2=Birmpas |first2=Georgios |last3=Filos-Ratsikas |first3=Aris |last4=Hollender |first4=Alexandros |last5=Voudouris |first5=Alexandros A. |date=8 April 2021 |title=Maximum Nash welfare and other stories about EFX |journal=Theoretical Computer Science |volume=863 |pages=69–85 |doi=10.1016/j.tcs.2021.02.020 |arxiv=2001.09838 }}</ref>

When all agents share one of two possible additive valuation functions, EFX was shown to always exist;<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Mahara |first=Ryoga |date=15 December 2023 |title=Existence of EFX for two additive valuations |journal=Discrete Applied Mathematics |volume=340 |pages=115–122 |doi=10.1016/j.dam.2023.06.035 }}</ref> this was extended to two monotone valuations,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Mahara |first=Ryoga |date=May 2024 |title=Extension of Additive Valuations to General Valuations on the Existence of EFX |journal=Mathematics of Operations Research |volume=49 |issue=2 |pages=1263–1277 |doi=10.1287/moor.2022.0044 }}</ref> and to three distinct additive valuation functions.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hv |first1=Vishwa Prakash |last2=Ghosal |first2=Pratik |last3=Nimbhorkar |first3=Prajakta |last4=Varma |first4=Nithin |title=Proceedings of the 26th ACM Conference on Economics and Computation |chapter=EFX Exists for Three Types of Agents |date=2025 |pages=101–128 |doi=10.1145/3736252.3742509 |isbn=979-8-4007-1943-1 }}</ref>

EFX is also known to exist for lexicographic preferences and for graph-structured allocation settings.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Christodoulou |first1=George |last2=Fiat |first2=Amos |last3=Koutsoupias |first3=Elias |last4=Sgouritsa |first4=Alkmini |title=Proceedings of the 24th ACM Conference on Economics and Computation |chapter=Fair allocation in graphs |date=2023 |pages=473–488 |doi=10.1145/3580507.3597764 |isbn=979-8-4007-0104-7 }}</ref>
